root_theorem.statement_nl:
Let $m_0$ and $n_0$ be distinct positive integers. For every positive integer $k$,
define $m_k$ and $n_k$ to be the relatively prime positive integers such that
\[
\frac{m_k}{n_k} = \frac{2m_{k-1} + 1}{2n_{k-1}+1}.
\]
Prove that $2m_k+1$ and $2n_k+1$ are relatively prime for all but finitely many positive integers $k$.

Then there exists K in Z_{>=1}, depending on m0 and n0, such that for every integer k >= K we have gcd(2 m_k + 1, 2 n_k + 1) = 1.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Define d_k = gcd(2m_{k-1}+1,2n_{k-1}+1). By reduced-form uniqueness, m_k=(2m_{k-1}+1)/d_k and n_k=(2n_{k-1}+1)/d_k, and each d_k is odd. Iterating the exact difference identity m_k-n_k = 2(m_{k-1}-n_{k-1})/d_k yields that every prefix product d_1...d_k divides 2^k|m_0-n_0|. Because the prefix product is odd, it already divides |m_0-n_0|. Therefore all prefix products are divisors of one fixed positive integer, so only finitely many factors d_k can exceed 1. Hence d_k=1 for all sufficiently large k. Since d_{j+1} = gcd(2m_j+1,2n_j+1), this means gcd(2m_j+1,2n_j+1)=1 for all sufficiently large j, exactly as required.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let a and b be positive integers, and let d = gcd(2a+1, 2b+1). Let m and n be positive integers such that m/n = (2a+1)/(2b+1) and gcd(m,n)=1. Then necessarily m = (2a+1)/d and n = (2b+1)/d. In particular, gcd(2a+1,2b+1) is odd.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all positive integers a,b, let d = gcd(2a+1,2b+1). If m,n are positive integers with m/n = (2a+1)/(2b+1) and gcd(m,n)=1, then m = (2a+1)/d and n = (2b+1)/d. Consequently d = gcd(2a+1,2b+1) is odd.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let
A = (2a+1)/d, \qquad B = (2b+1)/d.
Since d = gcd(2a+1,2b+1), the integers A and B are positive.

We first show that gcd(A,B)=1. Indeed, if some integer c>1 divided both A and B, then cd would divide both dA=2a+1 and dB=2b+1. But cd>d, so this would give a common divisor of 2a+1 and 2b+1 larger than their greatest common divisor d, a contradiction. Hence gcd(A,B)=1.

Now
m/n = (2a+1)/(2b+1) = (dA)/(dB) = A/B,
so cross-multiplication gives
mB = nA.

Because A divides nA, the equality mB=nA shows that A divides mB. Since gcd(A,B)=1, Euclid's lemma implies that A divides m. Thus there exists a positive integer t such that
m = At.
Substituting into mB=nA gives
AtB = nA.
Since A>0, we may cancel A and obtain
n = Bt.
So t divides both m and n. But gcd(m,n)=1, therefore t=1.

Hence
m = A = (2a+1)/d
and
n = B = (2b+1)/d,
as required.

Finally, d=gcd(2a+1,2b+1) is odd. For if d were even, then 2 would divide d, and hence 2 would divide both 2a+1 and 2b+1, impossible because 2a+1 and 2b+1 are odd. Therefore d is odd.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all distinct positive integers a,b, let d = gcd(2a+1,2b+1) (positive). Define m = (2a+1)/d and n = (2b+1)/d (integers). Then m - n = 2(a - b)/d. Equivalently, 2(a - b) = d*(m - n), so d divides 2(a - b).

lemmas.proof_nl:
By definition of gcd, from d = gcd(2a+1,2b+1) we have d \mid (2a+1) and d \mid (2b+1). Therefore the quantities
m = (2a+1)/d and n = (2b+1)/d
are integers.

Now compute directly:
m - n = (2a+1)/d - (2b+1)/d = ((2a+1) - (2b+1))/d = (2a+1-2b-1)/d = 2(a-b)/d.
This proves the stated identity.

Consequently, multiplying both sides by d gives
2(a-b) = d(m-n).
Since m-n is an integer, the right-hand side is divisible by d. Hence d \mid 2(a-b).

Thus both conclusions of the lemma hold.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m_0 and n_0 be distinct positive integers. For each integer k >= 1, define d_k = gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1), and define positive integers m_k,n_k by m_k = (2m_{k-1}+1)/d_k and n_k = (2n_{k-1}+1)/d_k. Then for every integer k >= 1, one has m_k - n_k = 2(m_{k-1}-n_{k-1})/d_k. Hence m_k != n_k for every k >= 0.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all m_0,n_0 ∈ Z_{>0} with m_0 ≠ n_0, define sequences (m_k)_{k>=0}, (n_k)_{k>=0} and (d_k)_{k>=1} by: for each k >= 1 set d_k = gcd(2 m_{k-1} + 1, 2 n_{k-1} + 1) ∈ Z_{>0}, and set m_k = (2 m_{k-1} + 1)/d_k and n_k = (2 n_{k-1} + 1)/d_k (these divisions are exact in Z). Then for every integer k >= 1 one has the exact integer equality m_k - n_k = 2 (m_{k-1} - n_{k-1}) / d_k, and consequently (by induction from m_0 ≠ n_0) m_k ≠ n_k for every integer k >= 0.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix any k >= 1. By definition,

d_k = gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1),

so d_k is a positive integer dividing both 2m_{k-1}+1 and 2n_{k-1}+1. Also, by the recursive definition,

m_k = (2m_{k-1}+1)/d_k,   n_k = (2n_{k-1}+1)/d_k.

Therefore

m_k - n_k
= (2m_{k-1}+1)/d_k - (2n_{k-1}+1)/d_k
= ((2m_{k-1}+1) - (2n_{k-1}+1))/d_k
= 2(m_{k-1}-n_{k-1})/d_k.

This proves the stated identity for every integer k >= 1.

Now we prove that m_k != n_k for every k >= 0 by induction on k.

Base case: k = 0. This is exactly the hypothesis: m_0 != n_0.

Inductive step: assume for some k >= 1 that m_{k-1} != n_{k-1}. Then m_{k-1}-n_{k-1} is a nonzero integer. Suppose, for contradiction, that m_k = n_k. Then m_k - n_k = 0, and by the identity already proved,

0 = m_k - n_k = 2(m_{k-1}-n_{k-1})/d_k.

Since d_k > 0, multiplying both sides by d_k gives

2(m_{k-1}-n_{k-1}) = 0,

hence m_{k-1}-n_{k-1} = 0, i.e. m_{k-1} = n_{k-1}, contradicting the inductive hypothesis. Therefore m_k != n_k.

By induction, m_k != n_k for all k >= 0.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Turns the one-step identity into a recurrence for differences and ensures the difference never becomes zero.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m_0 and n_0 be distinct positive integers. For each integer k >= 1, define d_k = gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1), and define positive integers m_k,n_k by m_k = (2m_{k-1}+1)/d_k and n_k = (2n_{k-1}+1)/d_k. Then for every integer k >= 1, one has d_1 d_2 ... d_k divides 2^k (m_0 - n_0). Equivalently, d_1 d_2 ... d_k divides 2^k |m_0-n_0|.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all m_0,n_0 ∈ Z_{>0} with m_0 ≠ n_0, define sequences (d_k,m_k,n_k)_{k≥1} by d_k := gcd(2 m_{k-1}+1, 2 n_{k-1}+1) and m_k := (2 m_{k-1}+1)/d_k, n_k := (2 n_{k-1}+1)/d_k. Then for every integer k ≥ 1, the integer product d_1·d_2·...·d_k divides 2^k (m_0 - n_0). Equivalently, d_1·...·d_k divides 2^k |m_0 - n_0|.

lemmas.proof_nl:
For each j >= 1, the definitions give
2m_{j-1}+1 = d_j m_j and 2n_{j-1}+1 = d_j n_j.
Subtracting these two equalities, we obtain

d_j (m_j - n_j) = 2 (m_{j-1} - n_{j-1}).

I claim that, in fact, for every k >= 1,

d_1 d_2 ... d_k (m_k - n_k) = 2^k (m_0 - n_0).

This stronger identity immediately implies the stated divisibility, because m_k - n_k is an integer.

We prove the claim by induction on k.

Base case k = 1: the claim is exactly the displayed relation above with j = 1, namely

d_1 (m_1 - n_1) = 2 (m_0 - n_0).

Inductive step: assume for some k >= 1 that

d_1 d_2 ... d_k (m_k - n_k) = 2^k (m_0 - n_0).

Apply the one-step relation with j = k+1:

d_{k+1} (m_{k+1} - n_{k+1}) = 2 (m_k - n_k).

Multiplying by d_1 d_2 ... d_k and using the induction hypothesis gives

d_1 d_2 ... d_k d_{k+1} (m_{k+1} - n_{k+1})
= 2 d_1 d_2 ... d_k (m_k - n_k)
= 2 * 2^k (m_0 - n_0)
= 2^{k+1} (m_0 - n_0).

So the claim holds for k+1. By induction, it holds for all k >= 1.

Therefore, for every k >= 1,

2^k (m_0 - n_0) = d_1 d_2 ... d_k (m_k - n_k),

and hence d_1 d_2 ... d_k divides 2^k (m_0 - n_0), as required.

Since each d_i > 0, this is equivalent to saying that d_1 d_2 ... d_k divides 2^k |m_0 - n_0|.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let N be a nonzero integer, and let e_1,e_2,e_3,... be odd positive integers such that for every integer r >= 1, the product e_1 e_2 ... e_r divides 2^r |N|. Then for every integer r >= 1, the product e_1 e_2 ... e_r divides |N|.

variables.role: given parameter (fixed)

variables.name: e_i

variables.role: universally quantified index for finite products

quantifier_order: ∀ sequences (e_i)_{i≥1} with each e_i ∈ Z_{>0} and odd
Assume: ∀ r ∈ Z, r >= 1, E_r | (2^r * |N|)
Conclude: ∀ r ∈ Z, r >= 1, E_r | |N|
domain_restrictions: N is a nonzero integer (so |N| ∈ Z_{>0})
Each e_i is an odd positive integer (so E_r is odd and positive for every r)
r ranges over integers >= 1
Divisibility is the standard integer divisibility relation (a | b means b is integer multiple of a)
2^r |N| denotes 2^r * |N| (not exponentiation ambiguity)
witness_dependencies: There are no existential witnesses in the statement; all quantifiers are universal or are an implication over universals.
The sequence (e_i) is fixed once chosen and may depend on N (i.e. e_i can be chosen with knowledge of N), but not on r other than by indexing; E_r is determined by (e_i) and r.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all N ∈ Z \ {0} and for every sequence (e_i)_{i≥1} with each e_i ∈ Z_{>0} odd, if for every integer r >= 1 the product E_r := Π_{i=1}^r e_i divides 2^r * |N|, then for every integer r >= 1 the product E_r divides |N|.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let E_r:=e_1e_2\cdots e_r for each integer r\ge 1. We must prove that E_r\mid |N| for every r\ge 1.

Fix an arbitrary integer r\ge 1. Since each e_i is an odd positive integer, their product E_r is also odd. Hence E_r is relatively prime to 2^r; that is,
\[\gcd(E_r,2^r)=1.\]
By Bézout's identity, there exist integers u and v such that
\[uE_r+v2^r=1.\]
Multiplying by |N| gives
\[|N|=uE_r|N|+v2^r|N|.\]
Now E_r divides the first term uE_r|N| trivially. Also, by the hypothesis of the lemma, E_r\mid 2^r|N|. Therefore E_r also divides the second term v2^r|N|. Since a divisor of two integers also divides their sum, it follows that
\[E_r\mid |N|.\]
Because the choice of r\ge 1 was arbitrary, we conclude that for every integer r\ge 1,
\[e_1e_2\cdots e_r=E_r\mid |N|.\]
This is exactly the desired conclusion.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Removes the powers of 2 from the cumulative divisibility invariant using oddness of the gcd factors.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let N be a positive integer. Let e_1,e_2,e_3,... be positive integers with e_i >= 1 for all i, and suppose that for every integer r >= 1, the product e_1 e_2 ... e_r divides N. Then only finitely many indices i satisfy e_i > 1. More precisely, if S = { i >= 1 : e_i > 1 }, then |S| <= floor(log_2 N).

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any fixed N ∈ Z_{>0} and any sequence (e_i)_{i>=1} with each e_i ∈ Z_{>=1} such that for every r ∈ Z_{>=1} the partial product P_r := ∏_{i=1}^r e_i divides N, the set S := { i ∈ Z_{>0} : e_i > 1 } is finite and satisfies 2^{|S|} ≤ N. Consequently |S| ≤ floor(log_2 N).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let L = floor(log_2 N). We prove that |S| <= L, where S = { i >= 1 : e_i > 1 }.

Assume for contradiction that |S| >= L+1. Then there exist distinct indices
i_1 < i_2 < ... < i_{L+1}
in S. Set r = i_{L+1}. For each j = 1,2,...,L+1, we have e_{i_j} > 1, and since e_{i_j} is a positive integer, this means e_{i_j} >= 2. For every other index i with 1 <= i <= r, we still have e_i >= 1.

Therefore the r-th partial product satisfies
P_r := e_1 e_2 ... e_r >= e_{i_1} e_{i_2} ... e_{i_{L+1}} >= 2^{L+1}.

By the hypothesis of the lemma, P_r divides N. Since P_r and N are positive integers, divisibility implies P_r <= N. Hence
N >= P_r >= 2^{L+1}.

On the other hand, L = floor(log_2 N), so by the defining property of the floor function,
L <= log_2 N < L+1.
Exponentiating base 2 gives
2^L <= N < 2^{L+1}.
In particular, N < 2^{L+1}, contradicting N >= 2^{L+1}.

This contradiction shows that S cannot have L+1 elements. Hence |S| <= L = floor(log_2 N).

Therefore S is finite, so only finitely many indices i satisfy e_i > 1. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m_0 and n_0 be distinct positive integers. For each integer k >= 1, let m_k and n_k be the relatively prime positive integers satisfying m_k/n_k = (2m_{k-1}+1)/(2n_{k-1}+1), and define d_k = gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1). Then d_k = 1 if and only if gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1) = 1. Equivalently, for every integer j >= 0, if one writes d_{j+1} = gcd(2m_j+1,2n_j+1), then d_{j+1}=1 exactly when 2m_j+1 and 2n_j+1 are relatively prime.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all distinct positive integers m_0,n_0 and for all integers k >= 1, define sequences by: d_k := gcd(2 m_{k-1} + 1, 2 n_{k-1} + 1), and set m_k = (2 m_{k-1} + 1)/d_k, n_k = (2 n_{k-1} + 1)/d_k (so gcd(m_k,n_k)=1). Then for every k >= 1, d_k = 1 if and only if 2 m_{k-1} + 1 and 2 n_{k-1} + 1 are relatively prime (equivalently gcd(2 m_{k-1} + 1, 2 n_{k-1} + 1) = 1). Equivalently, for every j >= 0, d_{j+1} = 1 iff gcd(2 m_j + 1, 2 n_j + 1) = 1.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix any admissible initial data and any integer k >= 1. By the given definition,

d_k := gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1).

Therefore the statement

d_k = 1

is exactly the same statement as

gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1) = 1.

Hence, for every k >= 1,

d_k = 1 if and only if gcd(2m_{k-1}+1, 2n_{k-1}+1) = 1.

This proves the first formulation.

For the reindexed formulation, let j >= 0 and put k = j+1. Then k >= 1, so by the definition of d_k we have

d_{j+1} = gcd(2m_j+1, 2n_j+1).

Thus the assertion

d_{j+1} = 1

is exactly the same as

gcd(2m_j+1, 2n_j+1) = 1.

Finally, by the standard meaning of “relatively prime,” the condition gcd(2m_j+1, 2n_j+1) = 1 is equivalent to saying that 2m_j+1 and 2n_j+1 are relatively prime. So d_{j+1}=1 exactly when 2m_j+1 and 2n_j+1 are relatively prime.

No further properties of the recurrence are needed for this lemma.
